edges.effect_quant: In REDS-II, absent iron stores at follow-up occurred in 27% of returning frequent female donors and 18% of returning frequent male donors, while the INTERVAL randomized trial of 45,042 participants found that more frequent donation lowered ferritin and hemoglobin and increased iron-deficiency-related symptoms and low-hemoglobin deferrals.
edges.population: whole-blood donors, including frequent adult donors and adolescent donors
edges.mechanism: Each whole-blood donation removes a meaningful amount of iron-containing hemoglobin, and repeated donations can outpace dietary repletion, especially in menstruating donors or people with low baseline ferritin. Shorter inter-donation intervals compound the deficit by truncating the recovery window.
edges.summary: The evidence that regular blood donation lowers iron stores is strong and unusually consistent across large cohorts and randomized interval studies. Donation frequency is one of the dominant determinants of ferritin in donor populations, and low baseline stores can persist for many months without supplementation or longer recovery intervals.
edges.caveats: This edge reflects donor iron balance, not a blanket judgment that blood donation is unhealthy overall. Risk is strongly modified by sex, baseline ferritin, age, inter-donation interval, and whether ferritin-guided supplementation policies are in place.

evidence.notes: Iron deficiency in blood donors: the REDS-II Donor Iron Status Evaluation (RISE) study.

evidence.citation: Partanen J et al 2019 PLoS One
evidence.notes: The effect of donation activity dwarfs the effect of lifestyle, diet and targeted iron supplementation on blood donor iron stores.
Efficiency and safety of varying the frequency of whole blood donation (INTERVAL): a randomised trial of 45,000 donors.

new_entities.name: Body iron stores
new_entities.description: The level of stored iron available in the body, commonly tracked with ferritin.
